label: Stable Curves of Genus Zero
notes: Appendix D, printed pages 619 through 652, builds the combinatorial domain theory behind stable maps. We treat marked spheres, their collisions, cross-ratios, and trees of components as one compact moduli space whose boundary is controlled rather than pathological, supplying the splitting machinery later used for Gromov-Witten invariants.

label: Configurations of Marked Points
notes: The open moduli space records n distinct labelled points on the Riemann sphere modulo the Mobius group. Because PSL(2,C) has complex dimension three and acts simply, fixing three points kills all freedom, so the quotient has complex dimension n minus three throughout genus zero.

label: The Cross-Ratio Coordinate
notes: Four labelled points carry exactly one essential invariant after the Mobius action. Normalizing three of them to zero, one, and infinity leaves the fourth as the cross-ratio, an explicit coordinate that is invariant under every fractional linear transformation, as the notebook verifies symbolically using an exact rational identity.

label: M_{0,4} and Its Three Punctures
notes: The cross-ratio identifies the four-point moduli space with the projective line minus zero, one, and infinity. Each forbidden value records two of the four marks colliding, so the open space is a thrice-punctured sphere whose missing points await the compactification described on the following slide.

label: Compactifying to Mbar_{0,4}
notes: Filling the three punctures with nodal configurations yields the compact space, itself a projective line. Each boundary point is one way to split the four marks two against two across a single node. Three unordered two-two partitions of four labels give exactly three boundary points.

label: Stable Curves as Trees of Spheres
notes: A degenerate domain is a tree of projective lines joined at nodes, carrying the marked points on its leaves. Stability demands every component hold at least three special points, marks plus nodes together. That valence condition eliminates continuous automorphisms and makes the moduli space a manifold rather than a stack.

label: Reading the Dual Tree
notes: The dual graph turns a nodal sphere into a labelled tree: vertices are components, internal edges are nodes, and leaves are marked points. The notebook draws a five-marked example splitting as one-two against three-four-five, then checks that both vertices satisfy the at-least-three special points rule.

label: Grothendieck-Knudsen Boundary
notes: The full compactification is a smooth compact complex manifold of dimension n minus three, stratified by stable trees. Codimension-one boundary divisors correspond to partitions of the labels into two blocks, each of size at least two, indexing the single-node degenerations that bound the interior configurations.

label: The Forgetful Map and Universal Curve
notes: Dropping the last marked point defines a forgetful map from the n-plus-one space onto the n-point space. Its fibers are the curves themselves, so this map is the universal curve. Stabilization contracts any component left unstable after deletion, giving the recursive tower linking all the spaces.

label: Psi Classes and Dimension Counting
notes: Each marked point carries a psi class, the first Chern class of its cotangent line. In genus zero a product of psi powers is nonzero only when the exponents sum to the dimension n minus three, where it equals the multinomial coefficient. The notebook tabulates these exact intersection numbers.

label: Why This Matters for Stable Maps
notes: Cross-ratios give coordinates, trees encode degenerations, stability builds a compact manifold, the Gromov topology governs convergence, and Keel relations turn boundary combinatorics into cohomology. Together these supply the genus-zero domains and splitting axioms that the main chapters invoke to define Gromov-Witten invariants.
